Limits and Deductibles Descriptions Location Coverage Level Applied separately to each coverage: • Building • Contents • Time Element / BI Options available: • Separate limits and deductibles per coverage • Combined coverage limit (Building + Contents together) • Combined coverage deductible (Building + Contents together) Important: • Combined limit does NOT require combined deductible User may choose: • Combined limit + separate deductibles • Separate limits + combined deductible Location (Site) Level Limits and deductibles apply to all coverages at a single location Covers: • Building • Contents • Time Element Overrides individual coverage totals if more restrictive Policy Level (Policy Layer) Applies to all locations under the policy Can be defined for: • Building policy coverage (Cover A & B) • Contents policy coverage (Cover C) • Time Element / BI policy coverage (Cover D) Policy-level structures may include: • Blanket limits • Blanket deductibles • Coverage-specific policy limits Blanket Limits & Deductibles Blanket limit → Applies to the entire policy Blanket deductible → Applies to combined losses across all locations Additional controls: • Minimum deductible (floor) • Maximum deductible (cap) Purpose: • Control the total effect of multiple location deductibles

Slip Coding.pdf — page 14
Financial Terms Review 14 Term Simple Meaning Real Property Insurance Example (CAT Modeling Context) Blanket Limit One single limit for all locations combined under a policy. A policy covers 10 locations across Florida with a Blanket Limit of USD 100M. If any location is hit by a hurricane, losses from all sites together cannot exceed USD 100M. Part Of Shows how much of a larger insurance layer the specific policy covers. Layer is USD 50M xs 50M. The insured buys USD 20M Part Of 50M. CAT modeler applies only USD 20M limit from the 50M layer. Excess of (Attachment Point) Losses are paid only above this threshold. Policy: USD 100M xs 25M. For hurricane loss of USD 40M, insurer pays 40 – 25 = 15M. Blanket Deductible One deductible applied to the entire policy (not per location). A global retail chain (50 stores) has Blanket Deductible = USD 5M. If multiple stores are damaged in a cyclone, all losses combined share one USD 5M deductible. Minimum / Maximum Deductible Policy Deductible cap when deductible is percent-based. Policy has 5% of TIV per location, but min = USD 250k, max = USD 2M. If TIV is low , at least 250k applies. For high TIV sites, max 2M applies. Coverage Value Sum insured for Building, Contents, BI. Location in Texas: Building = 20M, Contents = 5M, BI = 3M. These values go into RMS/AIR exposure inputs. Coverage Limit / Coverage Deductible Limit or deductible that applies separately to each coverage. BI sub-limit: USD 10M BI limit, even though Building/Contents are covered higher. During CAT modeling, BI loss is capped at 10M. Site Limit / Site Deductible Limit or deductible that applies to an individual location. Japan factory has Site Limit = JPY 2B even though blanket limit for policy is higher.

Incept and Expiry Dates Inception and expiry dates are usually shown clearly on the first few pages of the slip. If insurance is written as exactly 365 days (example: 01-Oct-2023 to 01-Oct-2024), change the expiry date to the previous day (30-Sep-2024). Enter both dates in DD/MM/YYYY format in the INCEPTDATE and EXPIREDATE columns of the ACC file. INCEPTDATE EXPIREDATE 1/1/2019 12/30/2019 1/1/2019 12/30/2019 1/1/2019 12/30/2019 1/1/2019 12/30/2019 1/1/2019 12/30/2019 1/1/2019 12/30/2019

Slip Coding.pdf — page 18
Line Size Each insurer has their own share (line size), but for CAT modelling we always assume 100% line. Normally the line is entered in the PARTOF column, but for modelling it should be shifted to BLANLIMAT. Enter ‘1’ in the BLANLIMAT column for every row (means 100% line). BLANLIMAMT 1 1 1 1 1 1
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 18

text:
Slip Coding.pdf — page 19
Policy Limits Policy limit (Blanket Limit) shows the maximum amount covered for each peril. It is usually written at the start of the slip under “Sum Insured”. Most perils share the same limit, but sometimes specific perils, regions, or locations have lower limits (sublimits) mentioned later in the slip. If a limit is written as “annual aggregate” , it cannot be modelled in RMS RiskLink however model in Risk modeler. Enter the policy limit in the PARTOF column in the ACC file. PARTOF 25000000 25000000 25000000 25000000 25000000 25000000
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 19

text:
Slip Coding.pdf — page 20
Excess Some policies include an excess, which appears after the policy limit in the slip. If the slip says “Excess of deductibles set forth below” , and the deductibles are listed in another section, then use the deductible rules explained in Deductible slides. Enter the excess amount in the UNDCOVAMT column of the ACC file. Aggregate excess cannot be modeled in RMS RiskLink however possible in RM. If a large deductible is called “self-insured retention” and is mentioned separately , treat it as an excess. UNDCOVAMT 25000000 25000000 25000000 25000000 25000000 25000000
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 20

text:
Slip Coding.pdf — page 21
Sublimits Sublimits give lower limits for certain perils, regions, occupancies, or specific locations. • Example: California EQ may have a lower limit than EQ in other states. If the sublimit is higher than (policy limit + excess), then we don’t need to capture it. If the sublimit applies to the entire peril (e.g., all Flood) or to all locations in that region (e.g., all CA properties for CA EQ), then enter it as a blanket limit in the P ARTOF column. If the sublimit is very specific (only some regions/occupancies/addresses), it must be added later using RiskLink Special Conditions. Not all sublimits can be modelled. Avoid things like boiler damage. Only capture: • Nat Cat perils (EQ, Flood, Wind, etc.) • Defined regions/countries. See the Zone and Tier Definitions folder in the inhouse guides folder documentation defining common peril regions • Defined occupancies (schools, warehouses, etc.) • Vehicles or fine art only if they represent 100% of the value at that location • Specific addresses/locations clearly mentioned
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 21

text:
Slip Coding.pdf — page 22
What Are Deductibles? Simple Meaning: • A deductible is the amount the insured must absorb before insurance starts paying. Why it matters in CAT Modeling: • Deductibles change how much loss attaches to the model. • They can be flat amounts or percentage based. • They vary by location, peril, region, occupancy, etc.
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 22

Types of Deductibles Type Meaning Example Notes Monetary Deductible (Flat) Fixed amount USD 100,000 per loss Same for all locations % Deductible Percentage of value or loss 5% of TIV Used in high- risk regions Site Deductible Applies to whole location Building + contents together Peril-specific Coverage Specific Applies to individual coverage Separate for CV1, CV3 etc Common for wind/quake Combined Coverage Single deductible for building + contents “Property Damage deductible” BI may still have separate time deductible Blanket Deductible (default) Special/Specific Deductibles Peril specific (EQ, WS, Flood) Region specific (States, Country , Tiers) Occupancy (Schools, Warehouses) Location- specific (Address)

text:
Slip Coding.pdf — page 24
Blanket Deductibles • The deductible section usually describes a blanket deductible that applies in the absence of specific special conditions. This blanket deductible is applied to any peril not implicated in special conditions. • This deductible may be phrased as “USD100,000 any one loss occurrence EXCEPT:” or “USD100,000 all other losses” . • Enter the deductible in BLANDEDAMT in the acc file. • Monetary blanket deductibles (i.e. not a % deductible) entered in BLANDEDAMT are applied to locations covered by a policy. • NOTE: % blanket deductibles applied in the BLANDEDAMT column of the acc file will be based on all location values, not just locations damaged. This is rarely used. BLANDEDAMT 0 0 0 0 150000 150000
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 24

text:
Slip Coding.pdf — page 25
Location Deductibles • We can apply deductibles to a location (site deductible) or on a unit of coverage at a location (location coverage specific). • There may be specific deductibles for selected regions locations. • In the loc file, filter for specific regions described in the slip (e.g. by state, occupancies or location name). • You may need to filter the loc file on specific criteria e.g. State, occupancy. • It is often useful to create columns USERTXT1 and USERTXT2. They values in these column are free for you to alter as you please to categorise criteria e.g. member names or location types. They will be maintained on import into RiskLink but will not affect any modelling outcome.
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 25

text:
Slip Coding.pdf — page 26
Site Deductibles • Site deductibles are deductibles that apply to a whole location, independent of coverage type (CV1, CV2, CV3). • Site deductibles are entered in the _SITEDED column in the loc file for a given peril (EQSITEDED, WSSITEDED etc). • Monetary values or % deductibles can be entered here (% in decimal format). • Filter for your selected criteria (e.g. California) and apply relevant deductible for that peril. • Site deductibles can be viewed within RiskLink in the Secondary Modifier tabs in the loc table for each location.
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 26

text:
Slip Coding.pdf — page 28
Site level Minimum & Maximum % Deductibles • If a percentage deductible is given with a minimum and/or maximum value, create a column for the TIV of each location in your highlighted criteria and order a based on TIV . • In a new column, calculate the resulting deductible with the relevant % deductible applied. • If the value is below the minimum, code the minimum deductible value in these cells. • If the value is below the maximum, code the maximum deductible value in these cells. • If the value is in between the min & max, code the % deductible.
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 28

text:
Slip Coding.pdf — page 29
Location Coverage Specific Ded • Deductibles may apply per unit of insurance, meaning the deductible is specific to coverage type (CV1, CV2, CV3). This is most typically seen in % deductibles. • Coverage specific deductibles are entered in the _CV1DED, _CV2DED columns in the loc file for a given peril (EQCV1DED, EQCV2DED etc). • Monetary values or % deductibles can be entered here (% in decimal format). • Filter for your selected criteria (e.g. California) and apply relevant deductible for that peril. • Coverage deductibles can be viewed in RiskLink in the loc table, within the coverage table for each location.
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 29

text:
Slip Coding.pdf — page 31
Combined Building & Contents Deductible • Sometimes deductibles are given as ‘combined coverage’ or ‘property damage’ , this refers to the combined coverages of buildings (CV1) and contents (CV2 ). • Combined coverage deductibles can be entered in the _COMBINEDDED column. • Remember , there may still be a BI time deductible given which must be entered in _CV3DED. • % Minimum and Maximum • Use the same methodology described in previous slides to apply minimum and maximum deductibles however, calculate resulting value with relevant % deductible applied to the sum of CV1+CV2 and CV3 on each location separately.
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 31

text:
Slip Coding.pdf — page 33
Policy Conditions Ability to define a policy that applies ONL Y to certain locations • Example: A policy that covers only California locations Ability to define a policy that covers all locations but applies limited coverage (limit/deductible) to a subset of locations (Sublimit) • Example: A $100M EQ policy with a $50M sublimit for California locations These are generally referred to as Special Conditions At the Policy Level • Ability to define a condition at the policy level • Ability to see which locations the condition applies to • Ability to manually select the locations the condition applies to (User explicitly selects specific buildings/locations) • Ability to use criteria to automatically identify locations the condition applies to Examples: • State Code = CA • Occupancy Type = Hospital • UserT ext1 = “High Hazard Zone” At the Location Level • Ability to see which conditions apply to each location (Each location shows the list of applied Special Conditions) • Ability to manually assign which conditions apply to a location (User can override or add specific conditions) Example 1 — Policy applies only to a subset • “Apply this EQ policy only to California buildings. ” Example 2 — Policy applies to all, but with a sublimit • “Policy limit = $100M, but only up to $50M can be used for California buildings. ” Policy Conditions
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 33

Steps 1. Select the policy row • Open the account you are modelling. • In the account table, click on the policy row for the peril you want to modify. • The selected row will be highlighted with an arrow. 2. Open the Special Conditions tab • At the bottom of the window, click the Special Conditions tab. ▪ Condition name ▪ Type of condition – sublimit or policy restriction ▪ Sub-condition of – used to indicate parent-child relationship ▪ Total limit – overall condition limit ▪ Deductible – condition deductible
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 35

text:
Slip Coding.pdf — page 36
3. Open the Special Conditions window • Click the “ … ” button in the Details column. • This opens the main Special Conditions setup window.
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 36

text:
Slip Coding.pdf — page 37
4. Enter the special condition details • In Condition Name, give your condition a meaningful name. • Enter Total Limit (if you are applying a sublimit). • Enter Deductible (monetary or percentage). • If you are applying a % deductible per location, enter the percentage here. • The second table in the window is used to define which locations the rule will apply to.
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 37

text:
Slip Coding.pdf — page 38
5. Choose the location- identifying field In the Field dropdown, select the criterion on which you want to filter locations. Examples: • Country • State Code • County • Location Number • Occupancy Type • UserText1 (useful for tagging locations with custom labels in the LOC file, e.g., “textile mills”)
title: Slip Coding.pdf — page 38

Slip Coding.pdf — page 46
Financial Flow Example Level of Payment Which Condition Applies? Limit Used How the Loss Is Determined (Same Logic as Screenshot) 1. Loss paid by Sub-condition LA County Sublimit $10M Paid amount = Loss (for LA County) or $10M (whichever is smaller). This is the first cap applied. 2. Loss paid by Primary Sublimit California Sublimit $50M Paid amount = Loss (California) + (amount paid under LA sub-condition), but capped at $50M, or whichever is smaller. 3. Loss paid by Policy Limit Full EQ Policy $250M × 50% = $125M participation Paid amount = Loss (all other CA + non-CA) + (amount paid under Primary Sublimit), but limited by policy’s share. 4. Loss not covered Outside all conditions — Any loss beyond the applied limits is not covered and is passed back to the insured.

text:
Touchstone construction class codes
Touchstone construction class codes Construction class codes help to determine the vulnerability of your risks to various perils. Touchstone provides a set of construction class codes that you use to describe the building material and/or type of construction used in your risks. Support for construction classes varies by country/region. See the related information links to learn about Touchstone construction class codes and to find out which construction class codes are valid for each supported country/region. Also, see the link for validation information for unknown construction / unknown occupancy combinations. For information about supported codes and limitations for specific models, refer to the model documentation that is available on the Client Portal . Note: Touchstone also supports non- Touchstone construction and occupancy class codes, although we always recommend translating non- Touchstone codes to Touchstone codes wherever possible before importing your data. For more information, see the topics about non- Touchstone codes in the Help provided with your Touchstone Client.
title: Touchstone construction class codes

text:
Touchstone construction and occupancy class codes
Touchstone construction and occupancy class codes The construction and occupancy class codes that you assign to each exposure have an impact on Touchstone analysis results. It is important to understand the two categories of codes that Touchstone supports. You must also understand which construction and occupancy class codes are valid for the countries or regions in which your exposures are located. For information about supported codes and limitations for specific models, refer to the model documentation that is available on the Client Portal . Construction class codes Construction classes describe the dominant structural characteristics of an exposure. A unique three- or four-digit code identifies each construction class. Touchstone defines and categorizes construction classes in either of the following ways: By the predominant structural material of an exposure, such as wood, masonry, concrete, or steel By the type of structure, such as bridges, equipment, mobile homes, or storage tanks For a description of each construction class and a list of the construction class codes that are valid for each country/region that Touchstone supports, refer to the " Construction class codes" topic. Occupancy class codes Occupancy classes describe the dominant function or use of an exposure, such as residential, commercial, industrial, or transportation. A unique three- or four-digit code identifies each occupancy class. For a description of each occupancy class and a list of the occupancy class codes that are valid for each country/region that Touchstone supports, refer to the " Occupancy Class Codes" topic. Construction/occupancy class code combinations Each model/peril supports a specific set of construction and occupancy class code combinations per country/region. For an overview of how Touchstone can handle invalid construction or occupancy class codes during loss analysis, see the "Behavior for invalid construction / occupancy class code combinations" topic. Contact your representative for additional information about valid construction
title: Touchstone construction and occupancy class codes

text:
Touchstone occupancy class codes
Touchstone occupancy class codes The primary codes for occupancy classes define the type of activity carried out in the risks included in a record. Touchstone support for occupancy classes varies by country/region. Use the best possible occupancy class code from the appropriate list of occupancy class codes for a particular country or region. The related information links provide information about the Touchstone occupancy class codes and about which occupancy class codes are valid for each supported country/region. There is also a link to validation information for unknown construction / unknown occupancy combinations. For information about supported codes and limitations for specific models, refer to the model documentation that is available on the Client Portal .

text:
Automobile construction codes
States , Verisk Severe Thunderstorm Model for Canada , and the Verisk Hurricane Model for the United States provide separate damage functions for standard automobiles and for automotive dealerships. The automotive dealer damage function (construction class code 261 with occupancy class code 312 or 313) assumes that the majority of the vehicles are parked outside in the open. Accordingly, for a dealership with the majority of the cars outside and few inside, we recommend coding all this exposure with construction class code 261 and occupancy class code 312 or 313. However, if the majority of the cars are inside the dealership, for example, a dealership in a city in which there are a few cars in a showroom, we recommend coding the automobile exposure as Content Coverage C , and supplying the appropriate construction and occupancy class codes for the dealership itself. Behavior for invalid construction / occupancy class codes
Behavior for invalid construction / occupancy class codes This topic describes how Touchstone handles import of invalid construction / occupancy class codes. Touchstone allows you to import all combinations of construction and occupancy codes, even if a particular combination does not produce loss during an analysis. However, if a location has a construction or occupancy code that is not a valid Touchstone -supported code, Touchstone does not import the location. If you try to import a location with valid Touchstone -supported construction and occupancy codes, but one or both of these codes is invalid for the country or region in which the location is located, Touchstone imports this location and notes the incompatibility in the import log. During a detailed loss analysis, Touchstone determines whether the construction and occupancy combination for each exposure is valid both for the peril/model for which you are analyzing loss and for the country or region in which each location is located. In Analysis Settings , under Financial Settings , For Invalid Con/Occ Pairs provides options for the action that you want Touchstone to take upon encountering an invalid combination: Ignore : The loss engine omits from the analysis all locations that have construction and occupancy combinations that are invalid based on region/country, model, and/or peril. In this case, Touchstone does not produce loss for these locations. To identify locations that were not included in a loss analysis, check the analysis log. Use System Default : During a detailed loss analysis, Touchstone remaps invalid construction and occupancy code combinations using either of the following construction and occupancy class codes, as applicable. In Touchstone 6.0 and later, Touchstone uses this option for each model individually within the analysis. Unknown construction ( 100 ) General commercial occupancy ( 311 ) Note: Touchstone does not remap construction and

Considerations for selecting the use system default option Before selecting the Use System Default option, which tells Touchstone to remap invalid construction and occupancy class code combinations to unknown/unknown or unknown/general commercial during a loss analysis, ask the following questions: Is it appropriate to use unknown construction and occupancy class codes to generate losses for the selected peril? Certain constructions or occupancies may not be vulnerable to a particular peril. For example, underground pipelines are not vulnerable to wind perils in Verisk models; therefore, it may not be appropriate to map an underground pipeline to an unknown construction and occupancy class code combination in order to produce losses. Is it appropriate to use unknown construction and occupancy class codes to generate losses for a particular construction or occupancy? It may not be appropriate to treat certain types of construction or occupancies as unknown. For example, industrial facilities react distinctly to wind or quake perils; therefore, it may not be appropriate to map an industrial facility to an unknown construction and occupancy class code combination in order to produce losses.

text:
Currency codes
Currency codes Currency codes supported by Touchstone during import. Before importing data, review the following information. To view the currency codes supported by Touchstone , log in to the Client Portal , navigate to the Developer Zone , click Touchstone Database Reference , and then search for "tCurrency Table" (located in the AIR Reference database). The Description field for the Currency Code column lists the ISO 3-character code for each currency. You cannot import data with, or set rates for, the following codes in Touchstone : ZWL, CYP, GHC, TMT, MXP, and CLF. You must convert these exposures to a Touchstone -recognized currency code prior to import. If you import exposures with the UF code, Touchstone will change the code to CLP, if you then export the data to a CLF. Since UF and CLP are different currencies, you should confirm the exchange rate in SQL before importing, or convert the exposure from UF to CLP before importing.

text:
Difference between Gross Area and Floor Area fields
Difference between Gross Area and Floor Area fields Gross Area and Floor Area are two different fields that are used in two different ways. Gross area may have an impact on loss estimates while Touchstone does not currently use floor area in any loss calculation. Think of the gross area as âsquare footageâ, where it represents the total square footage of the building. This value can have an impact on losses for the following models. Effect on Verisk Hurricane Model for the United States The vulnerability modification applies only to risks coded as: general residential (301); permanent, single-family (302); or multi-family (303) dwellings for which a building gross area above 3,000 square feet is also provided. Touchstone interprets the user-input square footage as the gross area of the building for both single-family (302) or multi-family (303) dwellings. Effect on Verisk Earthquake Model for the United States The vulnerability modification applies only to risks coded as: permanent, single-family (302); or multi-family (303) dwellings for which a gross area above 3,000 square feet is also provided. Touchstone interprets the user-input square footage as the gross area of the building for both single-family (302) and multi-family (303) dwellings regardless of the input of "number of risks" and "number of stories". Therefore, for multi-family homes (occupancy class 303), the square footage is for the entire building. Refer to the "Known Issues" section in the Touchstone Re release Notes, available on the Client Portal , for information about the required corrections when modeling high-value homes. Effect on Verisk Severe Thunderstorm Model for the United States For wind and tornado, the vulnerability modification applies only to risks coded as: general residential (301); permanent, single-family (302); or multi-family (303) dwellings for which a building gross area above 3,000 square feet is also provided. text:
Difference between Gross Area and Floor Area fields
Effect on Verisk Severe Thunderstorm Model for the United States For wind and tornado, the vulnerability modification applies only to risks coded as: general residential (301); permanent, single-family (302); or multi-family (303) dwellings for which a building gross area above 3,000 square feet is also provided. Touchstone interprets the user-input square footage as the gross area of the building for both single-family (302) or multi-family (303) dwellings. For hail, the vulnerability modification affects engineered and non-engineered buildings for which a gross area above 1,500 square feet is provided. Touchstone interprets the user-input square footage as the gross area of the building. Usage notes Most construction classes are supported except for 200-series construction types, manufactured homes (construction classes 191-194), and plate glass construction types (construction classes 185-187). While the modification applies only to Coverage Aâbecause coverage C and D damage is a function of coverage Aâthere will be indirect impact on coverage C and D losses. By contrast, Touchstone does not currently use the floor area value for any loss calculations; Floor Area is solely an informational field. Floor area represents the area of an individual floor of a building. Where the Gross Area value captures the total area of the building, the Floor Area value captures only the area of an individual floor of a building.

Term types
Term types Each of the financial terms (that is, limits and deductibles) that Touchstone supports for layers, sublimits, and locations fall into one of the categories indicated below. | Type | Description | | --- | --- | | ABCD | This category refers to financial terms that are split by coverage type (Limit A, Limit B, Limit C, Limit D). In very general terms, property exposure data treats these coverages as follows: A - Building B - Other Structures C - Contents D - Time For this financial term type, you import a separate replacement value for each of the coverage types and a separate limit to the amount of financial relief the insurance company provides for each of these coverage types. | | ABC-D | This category refers to insurance coverage that is split only between Building and Time coverage, where the Building accounts for the Other Structures and Contents together (Limit A, B, C, - then Limit D). This means that only a replacement value and a limit will be specified for A and for D separately, because B and C are being aggregated into A. | | Total | This category refers to insurance coverage that combines all exposure into a single replacement value and a single limit to the financial relief that the insurance company will provide. |
title: Term types

text:
Financial terms
Financial terms When working with policy terms in Touchstone , it is important to understand the financial terms that are supported and the combinations of the financial terms that are valid for running detailed loss analyses. The topics in these sections explain the financial terms, the criteria for specifying fields, and the valid combinations of supported terms and term types for layers, sublimits, and locations. Notes on Touchstone terms: Only one level of the Min/Max deductible is supported in a policy. If you import an exposure that has a sublimit within a layer, with both coded for MM (minimum and maximum), Touchstone converts the sublimit MM deductible into a blanket deductible. If multiple tiers of sublimits have MM deductibles, Touchstone converts the deductible on the lower tier to a blanket deductible. Touchstone supports multiple levels of aggregate terms. .

Location address fields
Location address fields Validation rules for fields related to the address of a location. Select an exposure view, a contract in the contract list, and then the Contract Details pane. You can select the area, sub area, and CRESTA zone from lists populated with values based on the selected ISO 2-character country code and, in the case of the Sub Area field, based on the selected CRESTA zone. When countries have both area and CRESTA zone information, the Sub Area field displays values only when there is a dependency between the CRESTA or Area fields and the Sub Area fields. (This change does not apply to 3-character offshore country codes.) In addition, the address columns have been rearranged in the user interface: Street, City, Country, Area, CRESTA , Sub Area, Postal, Geocode Match Level, Latitude, and Longitude. Note: If you select a country, such as âTogoâ, for which there is no information in the Geography database, and you then select the Area, CRESTA Zone, or Sub Area field, the list displays a blank field in which you cannot manually enter data. The only way that you can enter data in those columns is to make sure that they are included in the import file. When you change the Country (ISO Code) in the Locations grid, Touchstone automatically clears the Area (State), Sub Area (County) and Postal fields. When you change the Area (State) field, Touchstone automatically clears the Sub Area (County) and Postal fields. When you change the Sub Area (County) field, Touchstone automatically clears the Postal field. If you change higher resolution address data, such as the latitude or longitude, Touchstone does not automatically backfill the lower resolution address data, such as the Area (State) value. Project Data > Exposure Views > {Select Exposure View} > Contract List > {Select Contract} > Contract Details > Locations Locations Tab fields Location Contract Fields Location Address Fields Location Offshore Platform Fields Location Values Fields Location Basic Building Fields Location Term Count Field Location Reinsurance Count Field Location Building Detail Fields Location Marine Fields Location Roof Detail Fields Location Wall Detail Fields Location Connection Detail Fields Location Surrounding Detail Fields Location Builder Risk Fields Location User Defined Fields Verisk BINS (added in version 11.0) Terms (Location Terms) Reinsurance (Location Reinsurance) Specifying multiple risks in a location record You can specify data on multiple risks in a single record if they meet the following conditions: All the risks are at the same location. That is, all the risks have the same area , sub area , and postal area values. All the risks have essentially identical location-level insurance conditions. That is, all the risks have essentially the same replacement values , sums insured values, deductibles, etc. All the risks have essentially identical structural characteristics, that is, the same construction , occupancy , age , height , etc. In other words, all the risks must be homogeneous. If the risks are not homogeneous, then you must define each risk in a record of its own. Combining heterogeneous risks in a single record can produce incorrect results. When combining risks, make sure to enter the total number of risks in the Number of Risks field. Entering a correct value in this field ensures that the claims count, if selected in the analysis options, will be accurate.

text:
Using occupancy class codes
Using occupancy class codes Use the following information to understand how to choose occupancy class codes. When choosing between a 300-series code and a 400-series code, you need to be aware of some key differences that require knowledge of the facility and what the policy terms cover (the entire facility or the main buildings at a site). The 300-series codes are tuned to account for losses stemming from primary industrial structuresâthe actual buildings or major structures at an industrial site; they are not tuned for secondary structures such as tanks, manufacturing equipment, etc. The 400-series codes account for the secondary structures using a component-based approach to evaluate damage to an entire industrial facility, including the elements listed above. From a coding perspective, there is no distinct construction code associated with a 400-series occupancy; they are modeled with unknown construction. For information about modeling large industrial facilities, refer to Providing a Reliable Solution for Modeling Large Industrial Facilities on the Client Portal . Industrial buildings have features that make them generally more vulnerable to damage than other types of buildings, given the same construction types. These features include larger windows or doors, longer roof spans, and roof cover types that are more vulnerable to winds. Within the class of industrial buildings there is also variation in wind vulnerability. Light-metal buildings have been observed to be significantly vulnerable to damage by moderate- to high-level winds compared to concrete and steel-frame buildings. Similarly, wood and masonry constructions are generally more vulnerable to winds than the concrete and steel-frame buildings. The new Verisk Hurricane Model for the United States captures these variations explicitly. Compared to the previous version of the Verisk Hurricane Model for the United States , the wind vulnerability of an industrial building with an "unknown" construction type has not changed significantly;

Compared to the previous version of the Verisk Hurricane Model for the United States , the wind vulnerability of an industrial building with an "unknown" construction type has not changed significantly; that is, our understanding of vulnerability for a generic industrial building remains the same. However, since the previous version of the model does not distinguish between different construction types while the new model does, you will observe increases in losses for wood, masonry, and light-frame constructions, and decreases in losses for concrete and steel-frame buildings. Accordingly, depending on the mix of construction types for the industrial buildings within the portfolio, you may observe increases or decreases.

text:
Steel construction codes
Steel construction codes The steel construction codes supported by Touchstone . In Touchstone 2025 , we support codes 151-159 for Verisk Bushfire Model for Australia and Verisk Typhoon Model for South Korea . For information about supported codes and limitations for specific models, refer to the model documentation that is available on the Client Portal . | Construction code | Category | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | 151 | Steel | Steel frame buildings consist of steel columns and beams. Use this if the other technical characteristics of the building are unknown. | | 152 | Light Metal | Light metal buildings are made of light gauge steel frame and are usually clad with lightweight metal or asbestos siding and roof, often corrugated. They typically are low-rise structures. | | 153 | Braced Steel Frame | Buildings constructed with steel columns and beams that are braced with diagonal steel members to resist lateral forces. | | 154 | Steel MRF - Perimeter | Buildings constructed with steel columns and beams that use only the frame members on the periphery of the structure to carry lateral loads. The internal beams and columns only carry the gravity load to the foundation. | | 155 | Steel MRF - Distributed | Buildings constructed with steel columns and beams to carry lateral loads distributed throughout the building. The diaphragms are usually concrete, sometimes over steel decking. This structural type is seldom used for low-rise buildings. | | 156 | Steel MRF | Steel MRF buildings consist of structural steel columns and beams. Lateral loads due to earthquakes are carried by the "moment-resisting frames," but the locations of the moment-resisting frames in the building are unknown. | | 157 | Steel Frame with URM | Structural steel columns and beams
title: Steel construction codes

text:
Steel construction codes
Steel MRF | Steel MRF buildings consist of structural steel columns and beams. Lateral loads due to earthquakes are carried by the "moment-resisting frames," but the locations of the moment-resisting frames in the building are unknown. | | 157 | Steel Frame with URM | Structural steel columns and beams form "moment-resisting frames" to carry lateral loads due to earthquakes. Unreinforced masonry walls are used as infills between the columns to add lateral load resistance, but are not intended to serve as vertical load-bearing elements. Sometimes the steel frames are completely hidden in the masonry walls. | | 158 | Steel Frame with Concrete Shear Wall | Structural steel columns and beams form exterior frames, but the joints are not designed for moment resistance. Lateral loads due to earthquakes are carried by reinforced concrete "shear" walls. The concrete walls are continuous from the foundation to the roof. | | 159 | Steel Reinforced Concrete | Structural steel sections (beams and columns) are encased in reinforced concrete. The encased structural steel columns are sometimes discontinued in the upper portions of the buildings, making the columns in the upper floor regular reinforced concrete columns. | | 160 | Steel Long Span | Steel long-span buildings create unobstructed, column-free spaces greater than 100 feet for a variety of activities or functions. These include activities where visibility is important for large audiences (e.g., auditoriums and covered stadiums), where flexibility is important (e.g., exhibition halls and certain types of manufacturing facilities), and where large movable objects are housed. Two-hinge (made of a single member hinged at each end) and three-hinge (made of two members hinged at each end and at the meeting point at the crown) trussed arches are widely used. |
title: Steel construction codes

Contents (2): Building and contents payouts are based only on contents damage. Building and Contents (3): Payout is based on combined building and contents damage. The values are then visible in the Trigger by Amount section in the Content Start and Content End fields for trigger type 4 (Building, then Contents). This enables users to specify contents amount steps in addition to building amount steps for building damage, not just percentage and amount steps. text:
Terms (location terms)
Terms (location terms) Validation rules for for Touchstone terms related to a location. Select an exposure view, a contract in the contract list, the Contract Details pane, the location, and then the terms. In Touchstone 2024, we automatically map many Open Exposure Data (OED) financial terms to the appropriate Touchstone terms (policy, layer, and reinsurance).This ensures that you can model OED terms in Touchstone . For example: we currently map site and by coverage limit types, location participation, and site and by coverage deductibles We also map blanket and excess limit types and deductibles for layers, limit by coverage for sublimits, and some reinsurance data for layers. Note: You can define multiple coverage term sets for a location, each one based on a unique combination of peril, limits, and deductibles. You can include a particular peril only once in the entire series of coverage term sets for a location. When you use ImportExpress to import locations, you can define up to six coverage term sets for each location; this limit does not exist when you define coverage term sets for a location using the Touchstone user interface. When importing locations, you can define multiple coverage term sets for a location by appending a numeric suffix, such as "1" or "-1," at the end of each field in each term set. For example, to import a location with two coverage term sets, you can specify "LocPerils1" in the first coverage term set and "LocPerils2" in the second coverage term set. You can add term sets from the Terms tab located at the bottom of the Locations tab. To add one or more term sets, open a contract, select the Terms tab and then click Add Term Set . Touchstone adds the term set columns at the far right of the tab.

text:
Differences between property and workers' compensation exposure data
Differences between property and workers' compensation exposure data Workers' compensation policies and certificates require special consideration at the policy/certificate and location levels. Differences between property exposure data and workers' compensation exposure data include the following: Exposure base: With property exposures, the exposure base is the replacement value. With workers' compensation, the exposure base is the number of employees. Workers' compensation medical and indemnity payments: Exposure data can include expected medical and indemnity payments for different types of injury and for the time employees are expected to be working. The models can use default values, which include both medical and indemnity (wage) losses. These are industry default values, as are the employee counts. Clients can include their own estimates of average medical and indemnity costs and employee counts, which then override the default model values. Workers' compensation losses always include medical and indemnity (wage loss) estimates. Workers' compensation exposure data, which must be included in the location file: Location details, including address, construction type, and building height, and, for the earthquake peril, occupancy and primary risk characteristics. Number of covered employees at the location. In addition, the data can include payroll and average wage, which Touchstone can use to derive the number of employees (by dividing the annual payroll by the average annual wage). The annual payroll must be greater than or equal to the average annual wage. Expected values of medical and indemnity payments for different injury levels, including death, or the model can use defaults. Percent of employees working day, evening, and night shifts, or the model can use defaults. The injury defaults vary by state, and the shift percentages vary by occupancy, according to industry estimates. To view the defaults, open the Administration Console , select Loss Defaults , and then select Wages and Benefits . Perils: Earthquake
title: Differences between property and workers' compensation exposure data

text:
Touchstone and UNICEDE
Touchstone and UNICEDE Verisk provides a public reference to support the validation of UNICEDE -format exposure data in Touchstone . UNICEDE , is just one (open format) exposure data formats used by Verisk for analyzing insurance contracts and insurance-linked securities. Refer to the model documentation on the Client Portal for detailed information about modeled perils, construction classes, and occupancy classes, for each model. Documentation for some Verisk models includes a document that serves as a guide to the secondary risk characteristics (SRCs) used in the model. SRCs are features of a building and its environment that have a significant impact on the buildingâs vulnerability to damage during an event. The SRCs are important contributing factors to losses sustained by residential, commercial, and industrial properties. You can search the Client Portal for SRC documents by typing secondary risk characteristics in the field.

What's new in the 2023 (11.0) validation reference
What's new in the 2023 (11.0) validation reference The 2023 (11.0) Touchstone Exposure Data Validation Reference includes information about support for additional codes in some models. New and updated models This release includes: An expanded list of models supporting marine damage functions. See the release notes for a list of model updates by version. Support for the secondary peril framework for select models, allowing you to more accurately code location-level terms by peril or sub-peril. Support for the import, storage, and filtering of user-supplied Verisk Building Identification Numbering System (BINS) IDs into Touchstone exposure location data via CSV files. You can import up to four BINS IDs per exposure locations. During import, Touchstone validates the Verisk BINS IDs format to confirm that it meets the valid Verisk BINS ID format. This feature allows insurers and reinsurers to identify whether an address represents a building, a unit in a building, a site, or a campus. You can display and use the data in exposure views, contract lists, location lists, and all associated filters. You can also create geocode match mapping sets to map the BIN geocodes to Touchstone geomatch levels ( Administration Console > Object Management > User Geocode Match Mapping Set ). We added Verisk BINS to tGeocoderCode . The Verisk Earthquake Model for the Middle East will be available in Touchstone in 2024. We are providing you with CRESTA , area, construction, occupancy, and peril codes now for the eight countries that the model will support. This will enable you to start importing and verifying the exposure data for these countries. The supported countries are: Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and United Arab Emirates (UAE).

What's New in Touchstone 2020 (8.0) validation reference
What's New in Touchstone 2020 (8.0) validation reference New and Updated Models The following models are new to, or have been updated in, Touchstone 8.0 ( Touchstone 2020). New and/or updated loss files are available for each of these models. Verisk Inland Flood Model for the United States Verisk Hurricane Model for the United States Verisk Earthquake Model for Australia Verisk Earthquake Model for the Caribbean Verisk Tropical Cyclone Model for the Caribbean Other Updates Caribbean updates enable you to import exposure data for the Caribbean countries for use with Touchstone 8.0 model updates for Caribbean countries. Changes may include changes in CRESTA , Area, and Postal names and codes; boundaries, and code formats; there may be new and deprecated names and codes. Support for city-level data import and geocoding has also been added for all Caribbean countries. This release supports local intensity event calculations for the Precipitation Depth sub-perils of the Tropical Cyclone perils for the Verisk Hurricane Model for the United States and the Verisk Typhoon Model for Japan . More Information The Scope of Model and Software Updates , available on the Client Portal , provides high-level information about model updates and updates to Verisk 's Industry Exposure Database .

EMM Custom Lines of Business

Custom lines of business are defined for each Touchstone Re Advanced Loss Modification (ALM) country where sums insured data is entered in the Exposures pane for the selected peril, year and currency. Because Custom LOB definitions are specific to each Touchstone Re environment, UNICEDE /2 files with Custom LOB exposures must use generic LOB codes (LOB1, LOB2, etc.). Also, Custom LOB exposures must be coded with the Coverage Code âCLâ in any UNICEDE /2 file.

Field separator
Field separator Field details supported by UNICEDE /2. A Field Separator identifies the character that separates two adjacent fields (or values) in a record (or a line) in the file body. Currently the comma is supported as a field separator.

File body
File body UNICEDE /2 file details. The body of the file follows the header section. Each record in the body represents a set of risks in: A given area (i.e., U.S. state or European country) or subarea (e.g. CRESTA zone) A given peril covered for those risks (e.g. earthquake) A given line of business (e.g. Homeowners for a U.S. ceding company) It is very important that you include all the subareas in which the ceding company writes business. The coverages provided for in each record are: B : Buildings only. In the US this includes coverages A and B C : Contents only. In the US this includes coverage C T : Time element only. In the US this includes coverage D BC : Buildings and contents combined (i.e., the two coverages cannot be separated). In the US this includes coverages A, B and C BCT : Buildings, contents, and time element combined (i.e., the three coverages cannot be separated) . In the US this includes coverages A, B, C and D A : Automobiles only W : Workers' Compensation or pandemic exposure PD : Physical damage (Gulf of Mexico Offshore Platform only) CROP : MPCI Agricultural and Crop Hail For each record, you must provide data on at least one of the following: No. of Risks Sums-Insured Values Premiums and Rates % Note: Files containing Market Shares must be created and imported separately.. Each record must have the following characteristics: Each field must be assigned a value. If unknown, enter the digit 0 unless otherwise instructed below. It is very important that fields whose values are unknown are not skipped . Individual fields must be separated by commas (as defined by the FIELD_SEPARATOR value in the header). Individual records must be separated by a new line code, namely the

File body
enter the digit 0 unless otherwise instructed below. It is very important that fields whose values are unknown are not skipped . Individual fields must be separated by commas (as defined by the FIELD_SEPARATOR value in the header). Individual records must be separated by a new line code, namely the ASCII CARRIAGE RETURN character followed by the ASCII LINE FEED character (as defined by the RECORD_SEPARATOR value in the header). Finally, for every set of records for a given peril and a given LOB code, there must be a record for the area total. For example, if the file for a Belgian ceding company that provides Windstorm coverage contains nine records for Residential Building , one for each of the CRESTA zones, then the file must contain a 10th record for BELGIUM as a whole (i.e., areacode 11-000). If the file also contains records for, say, the Commercial LOB, then there should be a corresponding BELGIUM level (i.e., 11-000) record. These area total (i.e., country total and state total) records serve as check records to verify that the software reading the data is doing so correctly . The fields in each record of a UNICEDE /2 file are listed on the following pages.

UNICEDE /2 file header File header details supported by UNICEDE /2. The HEADER section of a UNICEDE /2 submission describes the contents of the file. Each file must begin with a header section. Each row in the header begins with an asterisk (*), making the header easy to identify when reviewing the contents of the file. It is important that: All the items listed below be included in the file They be included in the same order Each line starting with the asterisk (*) must begin in column 1, (i.e., without leading spaces) Each item occupies a single line ending with CARRIAGE RETURN and LINE FEED. | Item | Description | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Marker | This identifies the protocol being used. It MUST be reproduced EXACTLY as shown. | UNICEDE -PUBLIC-2.9.0 * Verisk - UNICEDE -PUBLIC-2.8.0 UNICEDE -PUBLIC-2.7.0 | | Reference | This is the source where you can obtain documentation that explains the details of the protocol, a document like this one. | *REF = Verisk , Boston, MA 02116 | | SourceDate | The date on which this file was prepared for submission. The date value on the left of ":" is in the universal 8 character format YYYYMMDD, where YYYY is the year, e.g., 2019 MM is the month, e.g., 09 DD is day, e.g., 07. | UNICEDE 2.9: *SOURCE DATE = 20170701: 1 July 2020 UNICEDE 2.8: *SOURCE_DATE = 20160701: 1 July 2019 UNICEDE 2.7: *SOURCE DATE = 20100701: 1 July 2018 | | SourceCompany | Name of the company that prepared the file for submission | *SOURCE_COMPANY = ABC Reinsurance Intermediaries Inc. | | SourceContact | Name of the contact person. | *SOURCE_CONTACT = John Smith | | SourceAddressLine1 | The address of the contact person. |

text:
Introduction to UNICEDE/2
Introduction to UNICEDE /2 UNICEDE /2 allows primary insurers and their treaty reinsurers to exchange aggregate sums insured, risk count, payroll, premium, and other appropriate data in a format that can be easily imported. UNICEDE /2 files can be used to import aggregated exposure data into Touchstone Re . The standard supports country-specific lines of business and geographic detail. Refer to the following topics for more information: Countries supported by UNICEDE/2 UNICEDE/2 protocol UNICEDE/2 file header File body Refer to Historical material for older material associated with UNICEDE /2.

Market shares Market share details supported by UNICEDE /2. The format of the UNICEDE /2 file is slightly different to permit the importing of market shares. Sums insured, number of risks, and premiums must be imported separately using the standard File body format. Note: You can include records from multiple supported countries in one file by using Data levels and Area tag type 98 or 99 in the UNICEDE/2 file header . | Field | Name | Description | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | AreaTag | Identifies the area (i.e., country) and the subarea (e.g., county or CRESTA zone) in which the risks represented in this record are located. | The AreaTag value used must be consistent with the AreaTagType from the UNICEDE/2 file header . | | 2 | PerilCode | Identifies the peril covered for the risks in this record. | Note: The data in the fields that follow should represent this peril. Data for different perils should be reported separately in different records. | | 3 | LOBCode | Identifies the line of business under which the risks covered in this record are reported. | The valid Line Of Business codes vary by country. When reviewing the codes for a specific country, please note that the available lines of business are sometimes different for Market Share imports. | | 4 | Coverage | Identifies the coverages included for the risks in this record. | When importing market share data, the coverage code should be set to MS . | | 5 | NumRisks | When importing market shares, this field displays the market share value. | This value must be entered in whole units (i.e., not in thousands or millions). | | 6 | SumsIns | N/A |

UNICEDE/2 protocol
UNICEDE /2 protocol Verisk has designed the UNICEDE /2 protocol based on specific considerations. UNICEDE /2 protocol The contents of the file should be easy to read both by people and by computer software in virtually any operating system. It is particularly important that the information contained in a UNI CEDE /2 file be readable by people so that: the data can be proof-read easily, if necessary. the individual elements of the file can easily referenced. The protocol should be easily extended when necessary while remaining compatible with prior versions, if any. The file must be a pure ASCII text file. It may contain only the following ASCII characters: printable decimal ASCII values 32 through 126 non-printable decimal ASCII values 13 (i.e., CARRIAGE RETURN) and 10 (LINE FEED) The presence of any other characters may result in the software either rejecting the source file or in ignoring the character. THE ACTION TAKEN DEPENDS ON THE SOFTWARE and is not part of the UNICEDE /2 standard. File Structure The basic file structure contains two parts: The Header describes the contents of the file. The Body contains the actual data being submitted.

United States FIPS Codes FIPS codes for the U.S. supported by UNICEDE /2. Note: Do not use this scheme for CLASIC/2 data format files. This Area code scheme is based on the country code and the U.S. FIPS codes for states and counties. This scheme can only be used to identify U.S. states and counties. Click a state below to view the supported counties and their codes. Please note that: Each code begins with the three characters '01-'. This set of three characters is the country code for the United States. The leading zero is required . The next two digits is the state FIPS code. For example, the FIPS code of Arizona is '04'. The leading zero is required . The remaining three digits identify the county. The value used is the FIPS county code, which must be padded with leading zeros so that the county code occupies all three digits. For example, the FIPS code for Cochise county in Arizona is 3. In UNICEDE /2 it should be identified by three digits, as '003'. United States FIPS Codes FIPS codes for the U.S. supported by UNICEDE /2. Note: Do not use this scheme for CLASIC/2 data format files. This Area code scheme is based on the country code and the U.S. FIPS codes for states and counties. This scheme can only be used to identify U.S. states and counties. Click a state below to view the supported counties and their codes. Please note that: Each code begins with the three characters '01-'. This set of three characters is the country code for the United States. The leading zero is required . The next two digits is the state FIPS code. For example, the FIPS code of Arizona is '04'. The leading zero is required . The remaining three digits identify the county. The value used is the FIPS county code, which must be padded with leading zeros so that the county code occupies all three digits. For example, the FIPS code for Cochise county in Arizona is 3. In UNICEDE /2 it should be identified by three digits, as '003'.
